lessons.title: The Ending & the Moral
lessons.description: The pigs become indistinguishable from humans, the final commandment, and Orwell's moral.
lessons.content_html:
Chapter Ten: The Passage of Time

Chapter Ten opens with a time-jump. Years have passed. Many of the original animals who took part in the Rebellion are dead. Boxer, Snowball, Old Major, and Jones are all gone. Only Clover, Benjamin, Moses the raven, and ‘a number of the pigs’ remain from the revolutionary generation. The farm has new animals who have never known anything other than Napoleon’s rule — they accept it as normal.

Orwell’s description of Napoleon and Squealer is pointed: both have grown enormously fat. Napoleon weighs ‘twenty-four stone’ and Squealer is so obese his eyes are barely visible. Their physical transformation mirrors their moral corruption — they have literally fattened themselves on the labour of others. The farm now ‘possessed’ three horses besides Clover, a threshing machine and a hay elevator — the word ‘possessed’ is significant because it implies the animals are property once more.

Key Fact

The time-jump is a deliberate structural choice. Orwell skips forward to show the long-term consequences of the revolution’s failure. The new generation of animals, who never knew Old Major’s vision, accept tyranny as normal — Orwell warns that without historical memory, oppression becomes invisible.

The Final Commandment

The Seven Commandments have been progressively altered throughout the novel. Now, in Chapter Ten, they are replaced entirely by a single commandment painted on the barn wall in enormous letters:

‘ALL ANIMALS ARE EQUAL BUT SOME ANIMALS ARE MORE EQUAL THAN OTHERS.’

This paradox is the novel’s most famous line. It is a logical impossibility — if some are ‘more equal,’ then none are truly equal. Orwell uses this contradiction to expose the fundamental lie at the heart of the pigs’ rule: they have claimed to uphold equality while systematically destroying it. The commandment also serves as Orwell’s critique of the Soviet Union, where the Communist Party’s promise of a classless society became a justification for a new ruling elite.

Original: ‘No animal shall sleep in a bed.’ Changed to: ‘No animal shall sleep in a bed with sheets.’ (Ch.6)

Original: ‘No animal shall kill any other animal.’ Changed to: ‘No animal shall kill any other animal without cause.’ (Ch.8)

Original: ‘No animal shall drink alcohol.’ Changed to: ‘No animal shall drink alcohol to excess.’ (Ch.8)

Final replacement: ‘All animals are equal but some animals are more equal than others.’ (Ch.10) — All seven commandments are erased and replaced with this single paradox, completing the revolution’s betrayal.

The Pigs Become Humans

The pigs now walk on their hind legs. Napoleon emerges from the farmhouse carrying a whip — the very symbol of Jones’s human oppression that the animals rebelled against in Chapter Two. The sheep, retrained by Squealer, now bleat ‘Four legs good, two legs better’ — a complete inversion of the original slogan. The animals who remember the old days are too few, too old, and too afraid to object.

In the novel’s climactic scene, Napoleon invites neighbouring farmers — Mr Pilkington of Foxwood — to dinner at the farmhouse. The animals peer through the window and watch pigs and humans playing cards, drinking, and laughing together. Pilkington congratulates Napoleon on running a farm where ‘the lower animals did more work and received less food than any animals in the county.’ Napoleon announces that ‘Animal Farm’ will henceforth be known simply as ‘the Manor Farm’ — its original name under Jones.

Key Fact

The renaming of Animal Farm back to Manor Farm is the final symbol of the revolution’s complete failure. The word ‘revolution’ literally means ‘a complete turn’ — the farm has turned all the way back to where it started.

The Final Image

The novel ends with one of the most powerful closing lines in English literature:

‘The creatures outside looked from pig to man, and from man to pig, and from pig to man again; but already it was impossible to say which was which.’

This image is devastating. The pigs have become physically and morally indistinguishable from the humans they overthrew. Orwell’s allegory reaches its conclusion: the revolution has produced a new class of oppressors who are identical to the old ones. The ‘creatures outside’ — the ordinary animals, the working class — are left staring through a window at a world of power and privilege from which they are permanently excluded.

Pessimistic: The revolution has achieved nothing. The animals are worse off than under Jones. There is no hope of further rebellion — the new generation accepts tyranny as normal. Power always corrupts.

Realistic: Orwell was a democratic socialist who believed in equality but saw how revolutionary ideals were betrayed in practice. The ending reflects his view that Stalinism specifically — not socialism itself — had failed.

Optimistic (arguably): The quarrel between pigs and humans at the card game suggests that the alliance between the ruling classes is unstable. The animals are still watching through the window — perhaps awareness is the first step toward future resistance.

Orwell’s Moral

Orwell described Animal Farm as a fable. Like all fables, it carries a moral. Orwell’s warnings are multiple: that revolutions are vulnerable to hijacking by those who seek personal power; that propaganda and the manipulation of language can make people accept any injustice; that political apathy enables tyranny; and that without education, literacy, and the freedom to question authority, ordinary people will always be exploited by those who rule them.
lessons.exam_tip_html: The ending of Animal Farm appears frequently in exams. When analysing the final line (‘it was impossible to say which was which’), explain the allegorical meaning (the revolution has failed; the pigs are the new oppressors) and the structural significance (the novel comes full circle, fulfilling Orwell’s fable structure). For questions about the Seven Commandments, trace the full journey from original to final paradox. For the 34-mark essay, always state Orwell’s purpose: he is not simply telling a story about animals — he is warning readers about the dangers of totalitarianism, propaganda, and political apathy.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • ‘All animals are equal but some animals are more equal than others’ — this paradox encapsulates the complete betrayal of the revolution. The Seven Commandments, once the foundation of Animalism, have been systematically destroyed.
  • The final image of pigs and humans becoming indistinguishable completes the allegory: the revolutionary leaders have become identical to the oppressors they replaced. Napoleon carrying a whip and renaming the farm ‘Manor Farm’ confirms the revolution has come full circle.
  • Orwell’s moral is that revolution without education, accountability, and democratic safeguards will always be hijacked by those who seek power for themselves.

practice_questions.text: Read the following quotation: 'The creatures outside looked from pig to man, and from man to pig, and from pig to man again; but already it was impossible to say which was which.' How does Orwell use language to convey his message in this final line?
practice_questions.marks:
Upper band (3-4): Detailed analysis. E.g. The repetitive structure ('from pig to man, and from man to pig, and from pig to man again') creates a dizzying, circular rhythm that mirrors the futile cycle of the revolution — it has gone round and round only to end where it started. 'Impossible to say which was which' is the culmination of the entire novel's allegory: the revolutionaries are now identical to the tyrants they overthrew. 'The creatures outside' positions the ordinary animals (the working class) as permanent outsiders, excluded from power. The word 'creatures' dehumanises them further.
Lower band (1-2): Basic comments. E.g. It shows that pigs and humans look the same now.

practice_questions.text: 'Orwell creates a shocking and unexpected ending to Animal Farm.' How far do you agree with this statement? Write about: what happens towards the end of the novel, and how Orwell presents the ending.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (26–30 marks + up to 4 spelling/grammar)Critical, exploratory response. Students should argue BOTH sides. The ending IS shocking: the image of pigs walking on hind legs, carrying whips, and drinking with humans is viscerally disturbing. The final line ('impossible to say which was which') delivers a powerful emotional punch. HOWEVER, the ending is arguably NOT unexpected — Orwell foreshadows it throughout: the pigs take the milk (Ch.2), move into the farmhouse (Ch.6), walk upright is foreshadowed by the gradual humanisation of the pigs. The fable structure means the moral is inevitable. Orwell's use of dramatic irony means the reader has seen the corruption building — it is the ANIMALS for whom the ending is shocking, not the reader. The real shock is how completely the revolution has failed — the farm is worse than under Jones ('the lower animals did more work and received less food'). Context: Orwell is critiquing Stalinism specifically — the ending mirrors how the USSR under Stalin became as oppressive as the Tsarist regime it replaced.
Upper band (21-25) Thoughtful, developed response. Top band (16-20): Clear, explained response. Upper-mid band (11-15): Some explained response. Lower-mid band (6-10): Supported response. Lower band (1-5): Simple response.
spelling/grammar: 4 marks for consistent accuracy.

practice_questions.text: Starting with the final chapter, explore how Orwell presents the failure of the rebellion in Animal Farm. Write about: the ways the rebellion fails, and how Orwell presents the failure of the rebellion.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-8): Perceptive analysis. Chapter Ten presents the failure as total: commandments reduced to a paradox, the farm renamed 'Manor Farm', pigs walking upright with whips, Pilkington praising the 'lower animals' for working harder for less food. The word 'revolution' literally means 'a complete turn' — the farm has turned full circle. Orwell traces the failure through structural choices: from Old Major's utopian vision (Ch.1) through gradual corruption to complete reversal (Ch.10). The rebellion fails because: no democratic accountability, no free press, no education for the masses, and blind loyalty (Boxer's 'Napoleon is always right'). Context: Orwell believed the Russian Revolution's ideals were sound but were betrayed by Stalinist totalitarianism.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some relevant comments.
Lower band (1-2): Simple comments.

practice_questions.text: How does Orwell use what happens to the Seven Commandments to explore ideas about the revolution? Write about: what happens to the Seven Commandments, and how Orwell uses the Seven Commandments to explore ideas about the revolution.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (26–30 marks + up to 4 spelling/grammar)Critical, exploratory response. The commandments function as a barometer of the revolution's health. Initially, they represent Old Major's vision of equality and freedom — no beds, no alcohol, no killing, all animals equal. Each alteration represents a specific betrayal: 'with sheets' allows the pigs to enjoy human luxuries; 'without cause' permits political murder; 'to excess' permits drinking. The animals cannot challenge the changes because they cannot read — Orwell's point about the importance of education. The final paradox ('some animals are more equal than others') is the logical endpoint: a statement that means the exact opposite of the original principle. Structurally, the commandments provide the novel's framework — from seven principles of equality to one statement of inequality. Context: parallels the Soviet Constitution of 1936, which promised rights that were never honoured.
Upper band (21-25) Thoughtful response. Top band (16-20): Clear response. Upper-mid band (11-15): Some explained response. Lower-mid band (6-10): Supported response. Lower band (1-5): Simple response.

practice_questions.text: Starting with the scene where Napoleon carries a whip and the sheep chant 'Four legs good, two legs better,' explore how Orwell presents the theme of power and control in Animal Farm. Write about: how Orwell presents power and control in this scene, and how Orwell presents power and control in the novel as a whole.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-8): Perceptive analysis. The whip is the most powerful symbol in the novel — it was Jones's tool of oppression and now Napoleon carries it, completing his transformation into a human tyrant. The sheep's chant has been inverted: 'two legs better' replaces 'two legs bad,' showing how propaganda can make people support the exact opposite of their original beliefs. The sheep have been retrained by Squealer — their mindless repetition drowns out dissent, just as it did in earlier chapters. Across the novel, power is maintained through three methods: propaganda (Squealer), violence (the dogs), and the suppression of education (the animals cannot read). The ending shows all three working in combination.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some valid points.
Lower band (1-2): Simple comments.

practice_questions.text: How does Orwell use events in Animal Farm to explore ideas about revolution? Write about: some of the events in the book, and how Orwell uses these events to explore ideas about revolution.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (11-12) Critical, exploratory response. The Rebellion (Ch.2) is Orwell's depiction of a spontaneous popular uprising — it happens 'almost before they knew what was happening,' suggesting revolutions begin with genuine idealism. The Battle of the Cowshed (Ch.4) shows the revolution defending itself. But from Chapter Five onwards, the revolution is hijacked: Napoleon's dogs represent military force, Squealer represents propaganda, and the changing commandments represent the erosion of founding principles. Each event moves the farm further from Old Major's vision. The ending — pigs and humans indistinguishable — shows Orwell's central argument: revolution without democratic safeguards produces new tyrants. The literal meaning of 'revolution' (a full turn) is fulfilled: the farm returns to where it started. Context: Orwell was critiquing not revolution itself but how the Russian Revolution was corrupted by Stalinist totalitarianism.
Upper band (9-10) Thoughtful response.
Top band (7-8): Clear response.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Explained response.

glossary_terms.definition: A gradual decline in moral character, principles, or integrity, especially in those who hold power.
